answer: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Special Education and Accessibility
children.blurb: A review of research on AI with students with disabilities found something uncomfortable. Much of the work described AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students, rather than as a way to empower the students and their families (Rice, 2023).

children.name: English Learners and Newcomers
children.blurb: In a trial with 217 second graders learning English, most of them Latino, a computer tutor taught the vocabulary of science and social studies units. Students who used it learned more of the taught words than students who did not, with an effect of 0.38 (Baker et al., 2020).

children.name: Communicating With Families
children.blurb: A school district once had a problem with truancy notices. The letters sent to families were written in legal language, warning of consequences and citing the education code.

children.name: Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety
children.blurb: A study of 14 companies that monitor students online found that most watch students around the clock, not just during school hours. Most use AI to flag concerning content, but fewer than half described any human review of those flags.

children.name: Counseling, College, and Career
children.blurb: Every spring, many high school graduates are admitted to college, plan to go, and never show up in the fall. Researchers call this summer melt.

sections.body: This part of school life covers the students and families who need the most careful attention, and the book groups that work into five areas: special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. AI shows up here in practical ways, such as messages sent to families and support given to students after high school. These are the places where the book says the strongest evidence in the Volume sits, including several randomized trials. The work is not about new subjects but about the students and families most easily missed.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, according to the book, includes messaging to families and support for students once they leave high school, both backed by randomized trials. What does not work is letting AI take over decisions that belong to people, and the book holds firm rules about which decisions must stay human. The rule it keeps is that these students and families get the most careful attention, so tools support the adults rather than replace their judgment. The evidence here is among the strongest in the Volume, which is why the rules are stated so firmly.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages fit together as one arc from the classroom to life after school. A teacher would go to Special Education and Accessibility and to English Learners and Newcomers for the day to day work with students who need the most care. A leader would go to Communicating With Families and to Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety for the systems that keep families informed and students safe. A parent or a counselor would go to Counseling, College, and Career for the path after high school, which the book ties to some of its strongest trials.
